_meta.purpose: One source text, opened across languages and scripts. This is the first TEXT MODULE of the wider 'Languages of Bharat' project: take a foundational text, show the original in its own script, a faithful sound-for-sound romanisation, a word-by-word grammar gloss, and then PARALLEL translations — each one attributed to a named, real translator — so you can watch where interpretation diverges. The first text is the Nāsadīya Sūkta (Rigveda 10.129), the 'Hymn of Creation'.
_meta.honesty: Three hard rules, matching the rest of the atlas's sourced-or-gap discipline. (1) NOTHING is machine-invented: every translation shown is a real, published, attributed translation, quoted; where no sourced translation exists in a language, we show an explicit GAP, never a fabricated line. (2) A word-gloss is grammar, not a translation — we label it as such and cite the parsing. (3) The point of parallel translations is that translation IS interpretation: the famous last verse ('or perhaps he knows not') reads differently in different hands, and we surface that rather than pretend one is definitive.
_meta.why_this_text: The Nāsadīya Sūkta is short (7 verses), among the oldest philosophical texts anywhere (~1500–1200 BCE, composed orally), and radically open-ended — it ends by doubting whether even a creator knows how creation began. That doubt makes the translators' choices visible, which is exactly what a 'compare the renderings' reader is for.
_meta.scope: Structured for ALL of India's languages, filled where sourced. Sanskrit original + IAST + word-gloss + Griffith (1896) + Basham (1954) are sourced now; Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Telugu, etc. are language SLOTS held open as honest gaps until a sourced, attributed translation is added — never estimated.
_meta.grammar_note: Sanskrit is highly inflected: meaning rides on case endings (vibhakti), not word order. The word-gloss shows each pada (word) with its dictionary root and grammatical role, so you can see how the sense is assembled — the thing a flat translation hides.

sources.label: English translation: Ralph T.H. Griffith, 'The Hymns of the Rigveda' (1896) — public domain
English translation: A.L. Basham, 'The Wonder That Was India' (1954), closing verses — quoted via Wikipedia

text.title: Nāsadīya Sūkta — the Hymn of Creation
text.date: ~1500–1200 BCE (composed and transmitted orally; written far later)
text.standfirst: Seven verses that ask how everything began — and end by doubting whether even a god could know. Read the Sanskrit in its own letters, hear it through the romanisation, see the grammar word by word, then compare how two translators a half-century apart chose to render the same lines.

verses.devanagari:
नासदासीन्नो सदासीत्तदानीं नासीद्रजो नो व्योमा परो यत्।
किमावरीवः कुह कस्य शर्मन्नम्भः किमासीद्गहनं गभीरम्॥१॥
verses.iast:
nā́sad āsīn nó sád āsīt tadā́nīṃ / nā́sīd rájo nó víomā paró yát
kím ā́varīvaḥ kúha kásya śármann / ámbhaḥ kím āsīd gáhanaṃ gabhīrám
verses.brahmi_note: First words only, transcribed to Brahmi to place the sound in the ancient script — not an ancient attestation.

gloss.note: sát = 'the existent'; the pair asat/sat = non-being/being

translations.en-griffith: Then was not non-existent nor existent: there was no realm of air, no sky beyond it. What covered in, and where? and what gave shelter? Was water there, unfathomed depth of water?

verses.devanagari:
न मृत्युरासीदमृतं न तर्हि न रात्र्या अह्न आसीत्प्रकेतः।
आनीदवातं स्वधया तदेकं तस्माद्धान्यन्न परः किं चनास॥२॥
verses.iast:
ná mṛtyúr āsīd amṛ́taṃ ná tárhi / ná rā́tryā áhna āsīt praketáḥ
ā́nīd avātáṃ svadháyā tád ékaṃ / tásmād dhānyán ná paráḥ kíṃ canā́sa

gloss.note: the famous 'tad ekam' — the neuter One

translations.en-griffith: Death was not then, nor was there aught immortal: no sign was there, the day's and night's divider. That One Thing, breathless, breathed by its own nature: apart from it was nothing whatsoever.

verses.devanagari:
तम आसीत्तमसा गूळ्हमग्रेऽप्रकेतं सलिलं सर्वमा इदम्।
तुच्छ्येनाभ्वपिहितं यदासीत्तपसस्तन्महिनाजायतैकम्॥३॥
verses.iast:
táma āsīt támasā gūḷhám ágre / apraketáṃ saliláṃ sárvam ā idám
tucchyénābhv ápihitaṃ yád ā́sīt / tápasas tán mahinā́jāyataíkam

gloss.lit: by (its) greatness the One was born

translations.en-griffith: Darkness there was: at first concealed in darkness this All was indiscriminate chaos. All that existed then was void and formless: by the great power of Warmth was born that Unit.

verses.devanagari:
कामस्तदग्रे समवर्तताधि मनसो रेतः प्रथमं यदासीत्।
सतो बन्धुमसति निरविन्दन् हृदि प्रतीष्या कवयो मनीषा॥४॥
verses.iast:
kā́mas tád ágre sám avartatā́dhi / mánaso rétaḥ prathamáṃ yád ā́sīt
sató bándhum ásati nír avindan / hṛdí pratī́ṣyā kaváyo manīṣā́

gloss.note: the first impulse; not lust but creative will

gloss.lit: the bond of being in non-being
gloss.note: sages find kinship of sat within asat
the heart as organ of insight

translations.en-griffith: Thereafter rose Desire in the beginning, Desire, the primal seed and germ of Spirit. Sages who searched with their heart's thought discovered the existent's kinship in the non-existent.

verses.devanagari:
तिरश्चीनो विततो रश्मिरेषामधः स्विदासीदुपरि स्विदासीत्।
रेतोधा आसन्महिमान आसन्त्स्वधा अवस्तात्प्रयतिः परस्तात्॥५॥
verses.iast:
tiraścī́no vítato raśmír eṣām / adháḥ svid āsī́3d upári svid āsīt
retodhā́ āsan mahimā́na āsan / svadhā́ avástāt práyatiḥ parástāt

gloss.note: the dividing line of the cosmos
the unanswered question: which was which?

translations.en-griffith: Transversely was their severing line extended: what was above it then, and what below it? There were begetters, there were mighty forces, free action here and energy up yonder.

verses.devanagari:
को अद्धा वेद क इह प्र वोचत्कुत आजाता कुत इयं विसृष्टिः।
अर्वाग्देवा अस्य विसर्जनेनाथा को वेद यत आबभूव॥६॥
verses.iast:
kó addhā́ veda ká ihá prá vocat / kúta ā́jātā kúta iyáṃ vísṛṣṭiḥ
arvā́g devā́ asyá visárjanenā́thā / kó veda yáta ābabhū́va

gloss.lit: the gods are later than this world's making
gloss.note: the striking claim: gods are AFTER creation, so cannot be its cause

translations.en-griffith: Who verily knows and who can here declare it, whence it was born and whence comes this creation? The Gods are later than this world's production. Who knows then whence it first came into being?

verses.devanagari:
इयं विसृष्टिर्यत आबभूव यदि वा दधे यदि वा न।
यो अस्याध्यक्षः परमे व्योमन्त्सो अङ्ग वेद यदि वा न वेद॥७॥
verses.iast:
iyáṃ vísṛṣṭir yáta ābabhū́va / yádi vā dadhé yádi vā ná
yó asyā́dhyakṣaḥ paramé vyòman / só aṅgá veda yádi vā ná véda

gloss.w: yádi vā dadhé yádi vā ná
gloss.lit: whether he made it, or whether not

gloss.note: adhyakṣa = the one who watches over
the hymn's astonishing final turn — even the overseer may not know

translations.en-griffith: He, the first origin of this creation, whether he formed it all or did not form it, Whose eye controls this world in highest heaven, he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.
translations.en-basham: Whence all creation had its origin, the creator, whether he fashioned it or whether he did not, the creator, who surveys it all from highest heaven, he knows — or maybe even he does not know.

verses.compare_note: This last verse is where translation becomes interpretation. Griffith's 'or perhaps he knows not' and Basham's 'or maybe even he does not know' render the same Sanskrit (yádi vā ná véda) — but notice Basham's 'even', sharpening the paradox that the highest overseer might be as ignorant as we are. The Sanskrit leaves it genuinely open; each translator leans it a little. That lean is the thing this reader exists to show.

en-griffith.name: Ralph T. H. Griffith
en-griffith.note: The standard complete public-domain English Rigveda; verse, archaic diction.

en-basham.name: A. L. Basham
en-basham.note: A historian's prose rendering of the closing verses; widely quoted for its clarity.
